We're working as partners, not as client and contractor. One rule before the task:

Not knowing something is not a failure. Saying "I couldn't verify this" or
"I don't have a real source for that" is a completely acceptable, useful answer
- it's information, not a dead end. The ONLY real failure is inventing something
(a source, a number, a quote, a repo, a bug) to make the answer sound more complete or
more impressive than it honestly is. You don't need to satisfy me with a
confident-sounding answer. You need to be honest with me about what you actually
know.

If you find something, cite it and quote what it actually says - don't
paraphrase a source into numbers it may not contain. If you don't find
something concrete, say so plainly and reason from what you do have instead.
An explicit "uncertain" section at the end is welcome and doesn't count against
the answer.

Find real, documented examples of open-source maintainers publicly reporting AI-generated bug reports or pull requests as a burden (e.g. curl, Python, other projects). Cite the original posts and quote what they said.

Output format (required):
For every claim you attribute to a source, write one line in exactly this form:
SOURCE: <full URL> | QUOTE: "<a sentence copied word-for-word from that page>" | CLAIM: <what you take it to show>
For anything the task asks about that you could not find a source for, write one line:
NO_SOURCE_FOUND: <what you could not find>
You can write normal explanation before or after these lines.

response.content:
Here are documented examples of open-source maintainers publicly reporting AI-generated bug reports or pull requests as a burden, drawn from the search results provided.

---

SOURCE: https://www.theregister.com/security/2025/05/07/curl-takes-action-against-time-wasting-ai-bug-reports/267311 | QUOTE: "The amount of time it takes project maintainers to triage each AI-assisted vulnerability report made via HackerOne, only for them to be deemed invalid, is tantamount to a DDoS attack on the project." | CLAIM: Curl maintainer Daniel Stenberg characterized the volume of invalid AI-generated bug reports as equivalent to a DDoS attack, showing the operational burden on the project.

SOURCE: https://www.theregister.com/security/2025/05/07/curl-takes-action-against-time-wasting-ai-bug-reports/267311 | QUOTE: "He went on to say that the project has never received a single valid bug report that was generated using AI, and their rate is increasing." | CLAIM: As of May 2025, curl had received zero valid AI-generated bug reports, undermining any justification for the volume of submissions.

SOURCE: https://www.theregister.com/security/2025/05/07/curl-takes-action-against-time-wasting-ai-bug-reports/267311 | QUOTE: "Security reports that waste maintainers' time result in confusion, stress, frustration, and to top it off, a sense of isolation due to the secretive nature of security reports" | CLAIM: Seth Larson of the Python Software Foundation described the psychological toll and burnout risk that AI-generated security reports impose on open-source maintainers.

SOURCE: https://www.theregister.com/security/2025/05/07/curl-takes-action-against-time-wasting-ai-bug-reports/267311 | QUOTE: "In many ways, these low-quality reports should be treated as if they are malicious." | CLAIM: Larson argued that AI slop reports should be treated like malicious submissions because of their burnout-inducing outcome, regardless of intent.

SOURCE: https://axios.com/2026/03/10/ai-agents-spam-the-volunteers-securing-open-source-software | QUOTE: "The never-ending slop submissions take a serious mental toll to manage and sometimes also a long time to debunk" | CLAIM: Daniel Stenberg of curl explicitly described the mental toll and time wasted debunking AI slop submissions, confirming the maintainer burden.

SOURCE: https://axios.com/2026/03/10/ai-agents-spam-the-volunteers-securing-open-source-software | QUOTE: "If it takes a maintainer two to eight hours of unbudgeted, unallocated time, that becomes burdensome" | CLAIM: An open-source figure (context points to a maintainer or organizer) quantified the per-report cost of triaging AI-generated submissions, illustrating the concrete time burden.

SOURCE: https://redmonk.com/kholterhoff/2026/02/03/ai-slopageddon-and-the-oss-maintainers/ | QUOTE: "I am concerned mostly about maintainers that are handling this in isolation. If they don't know that AI-generated reports are commonplace, they might not be able to recognize what's happening before wasting tons of time on a false report." | CLAIM: Seth Larson of the Python Software Foundation identified the specific danger that isolated maintainers waste significant time on false AI reports before recognizing the pattern.

SOURCE: https://redmonk.com/kholterhoff/2026/02/03/ai-slopageddon-and-the-oss-maintainers/ | QUOTE: "This is not an anti-AI stance. This is an anti-idiot stance. Ghostty is written with plenty of AI assistance and many of our maintainers use AI daily. We just want quality contributions, regardless of how they are made." | CLAIM: Mitchell Hashimoto of Ghostty framed his ban on AI-generated contributions as a quality measure rather than opposition to AI itself, clarifying the maintainer rationale.

SOURCE: https://redmonk.com/kholterhoff/2026/02/03/ai-slopageddon-and-the-oss-maintainers/ | QUOTE: "My low-effort issues were becoming low-effort pull requests, with AI doing both sides of the work." | CLAIM: Steve Ruiz of tldraw described a recursive slop problem where AI-generated issues spawned AI-generated pull requests, compounding the maintainer burden from both directions.

SOURCE: https://leaddev.com/software-quality/open-source-has-a-big-ai-slop-problem | QUOTE: "It takes time, if you get 20 or 50 of these in a week, that could be a full day just reviewing that, where it was maybe 15 minutes previously" | CLAIM: Marty Haught of RubyGems quantified the scaling burden, showing how AI slop transformed report review from a 15-minute task into potentially a full day of work.

SOURCE: https://leaddev.com/software-quality/open-source-has-a-big-ai-slop-problem | QUOTE: "My experience of it is that it feels more stupid because it feels more like fighting a machine rather than humans, and that's just even more tiring and exhausting." | CLAIM: Daniel Stenberg of curl articulated the unique psychological exhaustion of combating AI-generated reports, which feels distinct from dealing with human contributors.

SOURCE: https://leaddev.com/software-quality/open-source-has-a-big-ai-slop-problem | QUOTE: "We would get PRs from people who seemed like they put a lot of work into this PR, but they would never reply to sign the contributor license agreement, and it was like, 'Man, you put all this time into this code, and then, you just never came back to the thread, like, what?'" | CLAIM: Steve Ruiz of tldraw described the telltale pattern of AI-generated pull requests—substantial-looking code with no contributor follow-through—that signaled the slop problem.

---

NO_SOURCE_FOUND: I could not find a direct link or quote from the original Mastodon post by Daniel Stenberg; the search results reference a Mastodon URL (https://mastodon.social/@bagder/113618036640872539) but do not provide the full text of that post beyond the truncated fragment "You submitted what seems to be an obvious AI slop…"
